headings.title: Introduction to Structural Cardiac Disorders
headings.content: Structural cardiac disorders encompass a wide range of anatomical abnormalities affecting the heart's valves, walls, chambers, and great vessels. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding these conditions is vital because they contribute significantly to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality across diverse patient populations. These disorders can be broadly categorized into congenital anomalies—present from birth due to abnormal embryonic development—and acquired conditions, which develop later in life secondary to infections, degenerative processes, or ischemic events. Rheumatic heart disease, a major sequela of untreated streptococcal pharyngitis, remains a prominent acquired structural problem in developing regions like Nigeria, heavily impacting young adults and children. Conversely, congenital lesions such as septal defects or complex anomalies challenge neonatal and pediatric nursing units. Nurses must recognize that structural anomalies disrupt the normal mechanics of the heart, forcing the myocardium to work harder to maintain systemic and pulmonary circulation. This chronic strain ultimately leads to compensatory hypertrophy, ventricular dilation, and heart failure if left untreated. By studying structural cardiac disorders, nursing students build a foundational framework for identifying early clinical signs, participating in multidisciplinary care plans, and delivering culturally competent patient education suited to the local healthcare landscape. Comprehending the anatomy and physiology of these defects ensures that future nurses can anticipate complications, execute precise clinical assessments, and advocate effectively for patients navigating complex diagnostic and therapeutic pathways.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Hemodynamic Alterations
headings.content: The pathophysiology of structural cardiac disorders centers on how anatomical defects alter normal hemodynamics, pressure gradients, and blood flow patterns within the heart. When a structural anomaly occurs, such as a valve failing to open or close properly, or a hole persisting between cardiac chambers, normal unidirectional flow is compromised. This results in either volume overload, pressure overload, or a combination of both. For instance, valvular regurgitation causes blood to leak backward into a preceding chamber, creating a volume overload that forces the chamber to dilate and stretch its muscle fibers. On the other hand, valvular stenosis creates a narrow opening that obstructs forward flow, subjecting the upstream chamber to immense pressure overload and subsequent concentric hypertrophy. Similarly, intracardiac shunts like holes in the heart alter pressures by allowing blood to flow between the systemic and pulmonary circuits, depending on relative systemic and pulmonary vascular resistances. These hemodynamic shifts reduce the overall pumping efficiency of the heart, diminish cardiac output, and elevate central venous and pulmonary capillary wedge pressures. Over time, pulmonary congestion, systemic edema, and decreased tissue perfusion manifest as clinical signs of heart failure. Understanding these hemodynamic alterations helps nursing students connect structural flaws directly to the physical signs and symptoms observed at the bedside, guiding prompt clinical interventions and ongoing hemodynamic monitoring.

headings.title: Classification of Valvular Heart Diseases
headings.content: Valvular heart diseases are categorized fundamentally into two main pathological processes: stenosis and regurgitation, which can affect any of the four heart valves, though the mitral and aortic valves are most frequently involved. Stenosis refers to the narrowing or stiffening of a valve orifice, restricting forward blood flow and demanding higher pressures from the driving chamber. Regurgitation, also known as insufficiency or incompetence, occurs when the valve leaflets fail to close tightly, allowing blood to flow backward in the reverse direction. These conditions can be isolated to a single valve or present as multiple valve involvements in the same patient. Etiologies range from degenerative calcification seen in older populations to rheumatic fever damage, infective endocarditis, and connective tissue disorders. Nurses must be familiar with these classifications because each specific valve lesion produces distinct auscultatory findings, such as unique murmurs, and specific hemodynamic consequences. For example, mitral stenosis impedes blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle, elevating left atrial pressure and commonly causing pulmonary hypertension and atrial fibrillation. Aortic stenosis obstructs left ventricular outflow, increasing the risk of syncope, angina, and exertional dyspnea. Categorizing these diseases accurately enables healthcare teams to determine the severity of the lesion, predict symptom progression, and time surgical interventions appropriately before irreversible myocardial damage occurs.

headings.title: Congenital Structural Defects: ASD, VSD, and Tetralogy of Fallot
headings.content: Congenital structural heart defects originate during embryonic development and encompass abnormalities such as atrial septal defects (ASD), ventricular septal defects (VSD), and complex cyanotic conditions like Tetralogy of Fallot. An ASD is an opening in the atrial septum that allows oxygenated blood to shunt from the left atrium to the right atrium, leading to right-sided volume overload. A VSD involves an opening in the ventricular septum, creating a left-to-right shunt that increases pulmonary blood flow and can eventually cause pulmonary vascular disease if left uncorrected. Tetralogy of Fallot is a classic cyanotic congenital heart defect comprising four distinct anatomical abnormalities: pulmonary stenosis, a large ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. The combination of right ventricular outflow obstruction and a VSD allows deoxygenated blood to enter the systemic circulation, resulting in chronic cyanosis, clubbing, and acute hypercyanotic spells known as 'tet spells.' Pediatric nurses caring for children with these defects must closely monitor oxygen saturation levels, observe for signs of respiratory distress, and understand how to position a child during a tet spell—such as placing them in a knee-chest position to increase systemic vascular resistance and promote pulmonary blood flow. Early identification and surgical repair of these congenital defects are crucial for optimizing long-term growth, development, and survival outcomes in affected infants and children.

headings.title: Cardiomyopathies and Structural Remodeling
headings.content: Cardiomyopathies represent structural disorders of the heart muscle itself that are not directly caused by coronary artery disease, hypertension, valvular abnormalities, or congenital heart disease. They are classified into three major functional and structural phenotypes: dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and restrictive cardiomyopathy. Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by ventricular dilation and impaired systolic function, leading to a markedly reduced ejection fraction and weakened myocardial contraction. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy involves inappropriate and asymmetric thickening of the ventricular myocardium—particularly the interventricular septum—without significant dilation, which can obstruct ventricular outflow and create a high risk for sudden cardiac death in young athletes. Restrictive cardiomyopathy features stiff, rigid ventricular walls that resist normal filling during diastole, resulting in normal systolic function initially but severely compromised diastolic filling and elevated filling pressures. Structural remodeling is the common thread in these conditions, involving cellular hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and changes in myocardial architecture. Nurses must recognize that patients with cardiomyopathies are at high risk for heart failure, complex ventricular arrhythmias, and thromboembolic events due to sluggish blood flow within dilated chambers. Comprehensive nursing care involves monitoring for dyspnea, fatigue, peripheral edema, and implementing strict medication regimens alongside lifestyle modifications to slow down adverse cardiac remodeling.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Nursing Assessment
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of structural cardiac disorders reflect the underlying hemodynamic burden, reduced cardiac output, and congestion in pulmonary or systemic venous beds. Nurses performing comprehensive assessments must evaluate subjective complaints such as exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, dizziness, and anginal chest pain. Objective findings often reveal physical signs of heart failure and altered cardiac mechanics: elevated jugular venous pressure, peripheral pitting edema, hepatomegaly, and crackles or rales upon auscultation of lung fields. Auscultation of the heart may uncover abnormal sounds such as murmurs caused by turbulent flow across stenotic or regurgitant valves, as well as extra heart sounds like S3 or S4 gallops, which indicate ventricular volume overload or decreased compliance. Cyanosis and clubbing may be observed in patients with congenital cyanotic heart defects due to persistent right-to-left shunting. Nursing assessments should also include evaluating peripheral pulses, capillary refill time, skin temperature, and daily weights to track fluid retention. By systematically gathering these assessment data, nurses can grade the severity of symptoms using functional classifications, such as the New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional scale, and communicate vital clinical changes promptly to the attending physician or multidisciplinary team.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Imaging
headings.content: Accurate diagnostic evaluation is essential for confirming the presence, exact location, and severity of structural cardiac disorders. Electrocardiography (ECG) is frequently used as an initial screening tool to identify arrhythmias, chamber enlargement, and signs of myocardial ischemia or infarction secondary to increased workload. However, the gold standard for diagnosing structural heart disease is echocardiography—specifically transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Echocardiography utilizes ultrasound waves to visualize valve morphology, measure chamber dimensions, assess wall motion, estimate pressure gradients, and calculate ejection fractions in real time. Doppler imaging during an echocardiogram clearly maps turbulent blood flow, making regurgitant jets and stenotic narrowing easily quantifiable. When non-invasive imaging is inconclusive, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides exceptionally detailed views of myocardial tissue structure, fibrosis, and congenital anomalies with high spatial resolution. Cardiac catheterization remains a crucial invasive diagnostic procedure, allowing direct measurement of intracardiac pressures, visualization of coronary arteries, and exact quantification of shunt volumes or valve gradients. Nurses play a critical role in preparing patients for these diagnostic tests by explaining procedures, ensuring informed consent, monitoring vital signs pre- and post-procedure, and managing access sites for bleeding or hematoma formation.

headings.title: Medical Management and Pharmacological Therapy
headings.content: Medical management and pharmacological therapy for structural cardiac disorders aim to alleviate symptoms, reduce the workload on the heart, prevent disease progression, and manage complications such as heart failure and arrhythmias. Commonly prescribed medication classes include diuretics, such as furosemide, which relieve volume overload and pulmonary congestion by promoting urinary sodium and water excretion. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are utilized to lower systemic vascular resistance, reduce blood pressure, and slow down adverse ventricular remodeling. Beta-blockers are administered to decrease heart rate, prolong diastolic filling time, reduce myocardial oxygen demand, and improve survival rates in patients with heart failure or cardiomyopathies. For patients with structural lesions predisposing them to stasis and clot formation—such as mitral stenosis or atrial fibrillation—anticoagulant therapy with agents like warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants is critical to prevent thromboembolic strokes. Nurses must monitor patients closely for potential adverse drug effects, such as hypotension, electrolyte imbalances, and bleeding risks associated with anticoagulation. Patient education regarding medication adherence, dietary sodium restriction, and daily weight monitoring is a cornerstone of nursing practice, empowering patients to manage chronic symptoms effectively at home.

headings.title: Surgical and Interventional Procedures
headings.content: When medical management is no longer sufficient to control symptoms or prevent hemodynamic collapse, surgical and interventional procedures become necessary to correct structural cardiac defects. Interventional cardiology offers minimally invasive catheter-based options, such as balloon valvuloplasty to open stenotic valves or transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) for high-risk surgical candidates. Percutaneous closure devices can also be deployed to seal atrial or ventricular septal defects without requiring open-heart surgery. However, severe or complex structural anomalies often require traditional open-heart surgery utilizing cardiopulmonary bypass. Surgical options include valve repair—such as annuloplasty ring placement to reinforce regurgitant valves—or valve replacement using mechanical valves, which require lifelong anticoagulation, or bioprosthetic valves, which have limited durability but do not mandate lifelong blood thinners. Complex congenital defects, such as Tetralogy of Fallot, require open-heart surgical correction involving patch closure of the VSD and resection of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction during infancy or childhood. Nurses working in surgical settings must collaborate with the multidisciplinary team to ensure thorough preoperative stabilization, safe intraoperative management, and smooth transitions to specialized recovery units.

headings.title: Postoperative Nursing Care and Patient Education
headings.content: Postoperative nursing care following corrective surgery for structural cardiac disorders requires meticulous monitoring in a high-dependency or intensive care unit setting. Nurses must continuously monitor hemodynamic parameters, including blood pressure, central venous pressure, heart rhythm, and urine output, to detect early signs of hemorrhage, cardiac tamponade, low cardiac output syndrome, or arrhythmias. Respiratory management involves assessing breath sounds, managing mechanical ventilation weaning, and encouraging early mobilization and incentive spirometry to prevent atelectasis and pneumonia. Pain management is paramount, as adequate comfort facilitates deep breathing and coughing exercises. Surgical incision sites—whether a median sternotomy or catheter access points—must be inspected regularly for signs of infection, erythema, or abnormal drainage. Patient and family education before discharge is critical for recovery and long-term health maintenance. Nurses must educate patients on prescribed medication regimens, activity restrictions, sternal precautions (such as avoiding heavy lifting), recognizing symptoms of infection or heart failure recurrence, and the importance of scheduled follow-up echocardiograms. In the Nigerian context, providing culturally appropriate discharge instructions that account for local dietary habits, access to follow-up care, and community support systems significantly enhances patient compliance and long-term survival.
